top.line: Firing journalists to hire technologists moves publishers to packaging
top.para: Press Gazette counted at least 3,434 UK and US journalism job cuts in 2025, and 2026 is on the same scale. A hiring plan states where a publisher's centre of gravity is going: hiring for traffic leads to clickbait, while cutting engineers leaves journalism unenabled. A publisher needs both, plus AI-enabled graph roles.

short.line: A hiring decision is a publisher's real direction
short.para: Firing journalists moves the centre to repackaging inputs everyone has, and engagement metrics produce clickbait by construction, while cutting engineers fails the other way. Keep the journalists and tool them, and hire historians, cartographers, ontologists and librarians, plus engineers. Five outside counts reveal a publisher's real strategy.

centre.line: Hiring for traffic moves a publisher's centre to packaging
centre.para: Every organisation's centre of gravity is where its product is made, and in a news publisher that is the journalists. Hiring engineers who build provenance, graphs and versions strengthens it. Hiring for traffic and content operations moves it to packaging wire copy, press releases and trending topics, which is a different business.

measure.line: The metric is a hiring plan in disguise
measure.para: Measure engagement and the organisation reorganises around opening pages, producing clickbait whatever anyone intends. This site's metrics, paying after reading and reader-controlled signals, measure value to the reader instead. A publisher measuring that way would hire for being worth reading to the end and paying for afterwards.

spectrum.line: Packaging businesses are coherent but the room is shrinking
spectrum.para: Pure aggregators are honest about what they are, but the attention business is shrinking: Facebook referrals down 58% in six years, US newsroom jobs down 57% from 2008 to 2020, and 16,000 answer-engine fetches returning 10 readers. A normal media organisation must cover both the reporting and the stack.

engineers.line: Cutting engineers fails too: nothing enables the journalism
engineers.para: Without engineers there is no story graph, no checkable provenance, no versions, no surfaces for agents and no meter, so reporting is thrown away as a PDF. Jonathan Palmer: journalistic expertise creates the advantage. Engineers capture the value journalists create; without journalists there is nothing to capture.

hire.line: Keep and tool journalists; add graph roles and engineers
hire.para: Tooling should be handed over as making journalists better, never replacing them. Hire AI-enabled people as librarians, cartographers, ontologists and historians, plus engineers and AI product managers, and measure value to the reader. An unsourced parable: we hire the ones you let go, and today those are journalists.

outside.line: Five outside counts reveal any publisher's real strategy
outside.para: Count original share, sourcing, corrections, roles hired against roles cut, and the metric the publisher reports. Reach's 220 cut and 60 created is such a signal. On this site the result would be high original share and sourcing, corrections not yet propagating, agents plus one person, and almost no readers yet.

limits.line: Tracker figures are minimums, motives unknown, parable unsourced
limits.para: Press Gazette's UK and US figures are at least counts with no 2026 total. The argument concerns signals and metrics, not any publisher's motives, since some cuts are survival. The parable cannot be verified, and this small site is a working example of the stack, not proof at newsroom scale.

sources.line: Sources: Press Gazette's tracker and Tech Policy Press
sources.para: A voice memo of 12 October 2026. Job-cut figures from Press Gazette's 2026 journalism job cuts tracker; McClatchy detail from Chris Mills Rodrigo in Tech Policy Press, 8 October 2026; historical numbers via How news got here and Pew Research Center; and Jonathan Palmer's LinkedIn post of 10 October 2026.
